title: Battle of Changping
summary: In 260 BCE the state of Qin defeated Zhao at Changping, in today's Gaoping, Shanxi, after Zhao replaced Lian Po with Zhao Kuo and Bai Qi took Qin command. Wu's study, citing the Shiji, says about 400,000 Zhao troops surrendered and almost all were slaughtered, and that Zhao lost 450,000 in all; other scholars call the numbers exaggerated.

uncertainty.note: 260 BCE is the Shiji date for the battle (begun fourth month, ended ninth month); Wu notes Yang Kuan argued it began in 262 BCE and World History Encyclopedia lists 262-260 BCE.

as_recorded.value: The battle of Changping ended in the ninth month of the 47th year of Qin Zhaoxiang Wang (260 BCE)
In the battle of Changping (today's Gaoping, Shanxi) in 260 BCE

where.modern_name: Gaoping, Jincheng, Shanxi, China (proxy pin: Changping lay in the northwest of today's Gaoping)
where.historical_name: Changping, state of Zhao, Warring States China

importance.justification: A decisive Qin victory over Zhao whose reported losses are among the largest recorded for the Warring States.

sources.title: A Study on the Battle of Changping
sources.author: Leijia Wu

reviewer_note: Death tolls as sourced: Wu (citing Shiji) about 400,000 Zhao troops surrendered and nearly all killed, 450,000 lost in total; chinaknowledge repeats 400,000 buried alive; Qin losses unrecorded, modern scholars 250,000 to 500,000 per Wu, who thinks Qin losses were limited. Bodde and Lewis (cited by Wu) call the Zhao figure exaggerated. Pin is a proxy at Gaoping city; battlefield spans the area to its northwest.
